key_terms.meaning: The pattern of an array of identical elements with the element pattern removed; it depends on element spacing, phase and number.
Total far-field pattern = element pattern × array factor; valid for identical, similarly oriented elements.
N equally spaced elements with equal amplitude and a constant phase difference between neighbours.
Maximum radiation at θ = 90° to the array axis; adjacent elements have zero progressive phase (α = 0).
Maximum radiation along the array axis; adjacent phase shift α = ∓βd, where β = 2π/λ.
Non-uniform element amplitudes reduce sidelobes at the cost of a wider main beam.
Amplitudes proportional to binomial coefficients; no sidelobes for ideal isotropic elements, but broad beam.
Amplitude taper giving equal prescribed sidelobe level with the narrowest main beam for that level.
A constant phase difference α between neighbouring elements steers the main beam; phase shifters make a phased array.
A driven dipole with a reflector behind and directors in front; compact directional antenna.
Dipoles whose lengths and spacings scale by a constant ratio τ; wideband directional antenna.
The few log-periodic elements near resonance that radiate strongly at a given frequency.
A waveguide flared at its open end to match free space and radiate an aperture field.
A slot in a conducting screen has the same pattern as a complementary dipole, with E and H interchanged.
A paraboloidal surface that converts a spherical wave from a focus feed into a plane wave.
Feed geometries for parabolic reflectors: prime focus at the focus, Cassegrain with a hyperbolic subreflector, Gregorian with an elliptical subreflector.
Feed radiation missing the reflector is spillover; edge illumination relative to centre is taper; both trade gain against sidelobes.
A resonant metal patch on a grounded dielectric; fringing fields at its edges radiate.
Measuring gain, pattern and polarization at distance R ≥ 2D²/λ, where D is the largest antenna dimension.
The ionized upper atmosphere bends HF waves back to earth; this sky wave enables long-distance HF communication.

takeaways: Pattern multiplication lets you design an array by multiplying a known element pattern by an array factor.
A two-element array factor is 2 cos(ψ/2), with ψ = βd cosθ + α; nulls and maxima come from ψ.
Broadside arrays fire at 90° to the axis with α = 0; end-fire arrays fire along the axis with α = ±βd.
More elements and larger spacing narrow the main beam, but large spacing creates grating lobes.
Amplitude tapering lowers sidelobes; binomial removes sidelobes, Chebyshev gives equal sidelobes with controlled beamwidth.
Progressive phase shifts steer a phased-array beam electronically, without moving the array.
Yagi-Uda gives a compact fixed-frequency beam; log-periodic gives wideband operation through a moving active region.
A horn feeds free space efficiently; a parabolic reflector gives high gain and narrow beam, with spillover and taper trade-offs.
Microstrip patches are low-profile and cheap but narrowband; measurement in the far field verifies gain, pattern and polarization.
Ground, sky and space waves cover different frequency ranges; the ionosphere makes HF sky-wave links possible.
bank_note: Long answers stress derivations and comparisons: array factor and pattern multiplication, broadside/end-fire conditions, tapering choices, Yagi/log-periodic operation, horn/reflector/microstrip design, measurement setup and propagation modes.

bank.q: Explain pattern multiplication for antenna arrays and derive the array factor of a two-element array of equal elements spaced d apart with progressive phase α.
outline: State pattern multiplication: total pattern = element pattern × array factor.
Define ψ = βd cosθ + α and β = 2π/λ.
Derive AF = 2 cos(ψ/2).
Find maxima and nulls from ψ.
Sketch broadside and end-fire cases.

bank.q: Define broadside and end-fire arrays. Derive the phase condition for each and sketch their radiation patterns.
outline: Define array axis and angle θ.
Broadside condition α = 0 and maximum at θ = 90°.
End-fire condition α = ∓βd and maximum at θ = 0° or 180°.
Null directions and main-beam direction.
Pattern sketches showing beam position.

bank.q: Explain amplitude tapering in linear arrays. Compare binomial and Chebyshev arrays in terms of sidelobe level and beamwidth.
outline: Define uniform amplitude and its higher sidelobes.
Explain non-uniform taper and trade-off with beamwidth.
Binomial amplitudes and no-sidelobe property.
Chebyshev equal-sidelobe property and minimum beamwidth for a chosen level.
Comparison table of sidelobe and beamwidth.

bank.q: Describe the construction and operation of a Yagi-Uda antenna and a log-periodic dipole array. Define the active region of the log-periodic array.
outline: Yagi-Uda driven element, reflector and directors.
Parasitic element lengths and spacing effects.
Log-periodic scaling ratio τ and wideband behaviour.
Active region contains resonant elements.
Radiation direction and typical applications.

bank.q: Explain the radiation from a horn antenna and state Babinet's principle. Show how a slot relates to its complementary dipole.
outline: Horn as flared waveguide and aperture radiator.
Tapered aperture field and lower reflection.
Babinet's principle for complementary screens.
Slot pattern equals complementary dipole with E and H interchanged.
Sketch slot and dipole equivalence.

bank.q: Describe prime-focus, Cassegrain and Gregorian feeds for parabolic reflectors. Explain spillover and aperture taper trade-offs.
outline: Prime focus feed at the focus.
Cassegrain with hyperbolic subreflector.
Gregorian with elliptical subreflector.
Spillover from feed power missing the reflector.
Taper trade-off between gain and sidelobes.

bank.q: Explain the fringing-field radiation mechanism of a rectangular microstrip patch and outline its design steps.
outline: Patch on grounded dielectric substrate.
Fringing fields at radiating edges.
Resonant length about half a guided wavelength.
Substrate choice and feed placement.
Narrowband and low-profile behaviour.

bank.q: Describe far-field measurement of antenna gain, pattern cuts and polarization. State the far-field distance condition and precautions.
outline: Far-field condition R ≥ 2D²/λ.
Gain comparison with a standard antenna.
Pattern cuts in principal planes.
Polarization alignment and cross-polar measurement.
Avoid multipath and nearby objects.

bank.q: Explain ground, sky and space wave propagation. Show how the ionosphere bends HF sky waves and define critical frequency.
outline: Ground wave along the earth surface.
Sky wave by ionospheric refraction.
Space wave by line of sight.
Ionospheric electron density and bending.
Critical frequency and maximum usable frequency concept.

bank.q: Derive the array factor for an N-element uniform linear array. Find null directions and the grating-lobe condition, and explain phase steering.
outline: AF = Σ exp(j(n−1)ψ).
Closed form with sin(Nψ/2)/sin(ψ/2).
Nulls when Nψ/2 = mπ.
Grating lobe when ψ = 2mπ.
Progressive phase α steers the beam.

bank.q: Evaluate uniform, binomial, Chebyshev and phased arrays for sidelobe level, beamwidth and electronic scanning.
outline: Uniform array: narrow beam, higher sidelobes.
Binomial array: no sidelobes, wider beam.
Chebyshev array: controlled equal sidelobes.
Phased array: scanning without mechanical motion.
Trade-offs in radar and communication use.

bank.q: Compare Yagi-Uda, log-periodic, horn and parabolic reflector antennas for gain, bandwidth, size and cost in a practical link.
outline: Yagi-Uda: compact, moderate gain, narrow band.
Log-periodic: wideband, larger, lower gain than reflector.
Horn: efficient feed, moderate gain.
Parabolic reflector: high gain, narrow beam, larger size.
Choose by frequency range, bandwidth and installation constraints.

bank.q: Analyze a parabolic reflector link: choose feed geometry, account for spillover and taper, and verify gain and pattern by far-field measurement.
outline: Choose prime-focus, Cassegrain or Gregorian feed.
Relate spillover to feed pattern and reflector edge angle.
Relate taper to edge illumination and sidelobes.
Estimate gain from aperture area and efficiency.
Measure pattern in the far field and check polarization.

bank.q: Evaluate propagation mode choices for MF broadcast, HF sky-wave communication and VHF line-of-sight links.
outline: MF broadcast uses ground wave and local sky wave at night.
HF long-distance links use ionospheric sky waves.
VHF and UHF use space waves and line of sight.
Frequency, antenna height and ionosphere affect coverage.
Compare reliability, range and bandwidth.

glossary.def: The factor by which the element pattern is multiplied to give an array pattern.
The rule that an array of identical elements has total pattern equal to element pattern times array factor.
An array whose main beam is perpendicular to the line of the array.
An array whose main beam lies along the line of the array.
The ratio of the largest sidelobe to the main-lobe peak, usually in dB.
The angular width between the half-power points of the main beam.
A non-uniform amplitude distribution across array elements used to control sidelobes.
An array with binomial-coefficient amplitudes, giving no sidelobes for ideal isotropic elements.
An array with Dolph-Chebyshev amplitudes, giving equal sidelobes and minimum beamwidth for a chosen sidelobe level.
A constant phase difference between adjacent array elements that steers the main beam.
An array whose beam is steered by variable phase shifters or time delays.
A directional antenna with one driven dipole, a reflector and several directors.
A slightly shorter parasitic element in a Yagi-Uda antenna that increases forward gain.
A slightly longer parasitic element behind a Yagi-Uda driven element that reduces backward radiation.
A wideband array of dipoles with lengths and spacings scaled by a constant ratio.
The small group of log-periodic elements near resonance that dominates radiation at a given frequency.
An antenna that radiates from an open surface or opening rather than a thin wire.
A flared waveguide used as a directive aperture antenna and feed.
The diffraction pattern of a slot complements that of an identical conducting strip, with electric and magnetic fields interchanged.
A reflecting surface shaped as a paraboloid that collimates rays from its focus.
A reflector feed using a hyperbolic subreflector to place the feed behind the main reflector.
Feed power that misses the reflector and radiates in unwanted directions.
A printed resonant conductor on a grounded dielectric substrate.
The region at distance R ≥ 2D²/λ where the antenna pattern is essentially independent of distance.
The three main paths for radio propagation: along the ground, via the ionosphere, and by line of sight through the lower atmosphere.
The ionized layer of the upper atmosphere that reflects or refracts HF radio waves.
